title: Why the Moon Pulls You Toward It
narration: The Moon pulls harder on your side than the far side. The near side feels stronger gravity, the far side weaker. Earth bulges on both sides. Ocean water slides away from the crust toward the Moon. The crust resists, creating tension. The Sun pulls more overall, but the Moon is closer, so its gradient is steeper. That steeper gradient stretches you more. The Moon’s pull is what shapes tides. The Moon pulls harder on you.

title: Why the Moon, Not the Sun, Dominates Tides
narration: The Sun is 20 million times heavier, but it sits 400 times farther away. Tidal force drops with the cube of distance. The Moon’s proximity makes its gradient steeper. The Moon’s pull changes rapidly across Earth, while the Sun’s pull is almost flat. That steep slope creates a larger bulge. The lunar tide is twice the solar tide. The Sun’s tide is only 45 percent of the Moon’s. The Moon dominates the tides. The Moon dominates the tides.

title: The Distance Rule That Makes Tides Strong
narration: Tidal force grows with Earth's diameter and shrinks with distance cubed. Gravitational pull falls with distance squared, but tides care about the slope, which falls with distance cubed. A steeper slope means a larger difference between near and far sides. The Moon’s pull declines more steeply across Earth than the Sun’s. That steep gradient produces the larger bulge. The slope wins over total pull. The rule explains why closeness matters. The rule explains why closeness matters.
